blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's fine, thank you. I didn't need it earlier. It's all right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I should say the first two witnesses will be Jones and then Griffith chronologically, not Simcock.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
I call Tracey Jones, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: MS TRACEY JONES (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Can we start with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tracey Jones.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: I know I'm asking the questions. Can I ask you not to allow your voice to drop, please, and perhaps if you keep in mind that the ladies and gentlemen of the jury need to hear everything you say, if you can try and project your voice in that direction, we'd be very grateful.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. Your occupation, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm a senior lecturer in nursing.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. From time to time in that capacity do you work on a neonatal unit in order to maintain your competencies?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I did. I no longer do, but I did.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Did you do so back in 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: And in 2016, did you work a number of shifts at the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Tell us, please, about your qualifications.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm a registered children's nurse. I'm qualified in neonatal intensive care. I'm an enhanced neonatal nurse practitioner and an independent prescriber.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. Back in 2016, we've heard about various bandings and work allocation within a neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What band would you have been considered within the NNU?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Within the neonatal unit at Chester at that time, on my agency shift, I would have been deemed a band 5, but my other role was a band 8A.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. Were you qualified to care, for example, for intensive care babies?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: You've been asked or have you been asked to come along today to assist us with your recollections of a baby by the name of [Baby L]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Did you care for [Baby L] on the 8th and 9 April 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Do you have any independent recollection of [Baby L]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Only from reading my statement. I don't remember the baby.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: In preparing your statement, did you have access to the notes that you made at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Would it assist you if, during the course of your evidence, we refer to your notes as we go along?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, please.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Okay. Did you work a night shift on 8 April?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: We've heard that that would begin at 7.30 in the evening, there would be a handover, and you would then adopt sole responsibility for your baby at 8 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: I'm going to ask, please -- by way of assistance, if you look to your right there's a screen with a chronological presentation -- if we could go, Mr Murphy, please, to tile 53.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've agreed that that time is -- I don't think we need to go behind it -- is the time of the changeover.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just from your recollection and the notes generally, do you remember how [Baby L] presented when you took over his care at 8 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember unless I look at the notes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Okay. Perhaps if we then, please, to tile number 78.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we look behind that, that should show your nursing notes, albeit made at 04.27. Was the practice to make notes up when the opportunity arose and, if necessary, in retrospect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
This is actually your note?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: It is, is it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: If we just look at the top line with the date, I think we're becoming familiar with these. The initials that are shown are actually BB.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: And although it's shown as your note on our tile, would that be a note that you recall being made on your behalf?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It would be because I wouldn't have had access to the electronic system. So somebody would have logged in, probably, and allowed me to type in my note.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: All right. Does the B represent bank or would that be the initials of a particular nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Anyway, someone had to log on for you and then you created the note, so that BB is either some generic --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I can't --
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: No, don't apologise. The point is, it's got your name at the bottom, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, they'll be my notes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. You've obviously just taken the opportunity to cast your eye over them. Can I go through them with you, please. These hopefully capture, certainly up to 04.27, that particular shift:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Care taken over by T Jones, agency nurse, at 19.30. All safety checks completed and satisfactory. Fluids and enteral feeds checked and administered. Enteral feeds tolerated of donor..."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And we have learned that that's expressed breast milk.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: It then says:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Abdomen soft, passed meconium and urine."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Would they have been your observations?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Then you've made a note to say:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Cannula knocked out by baby therefore replaced by registrar."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Any recollection of that or is that just within the notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No memory of that, I'm afraid, sorry. It's a long time ago.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: There's then a reference to -- is that intravenous antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: "Administered as prescribed by ward staff"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Does that mean -- did you actually administer them or would someone else have done that on your behalf?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, because I was an agency nurse they would have done that.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: But as it's your baby, you record that in the notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: "Skin intact, no concerns. Full monitoring continues and observations within normal limits for gestation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Temperature maintained. Nursed in an incubator set at 32.5."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's presumably degrees centigrade?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: "Phototherapy continues, eyes protected."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And we've heard that is a treatment for jaundice --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: -- is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Again, related to jaundice, "Last SBR result", I think that's a bilirubin result; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: "... at 62 so lights to continue."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And you have noted:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Pre-feed blood glucose all above 2 mols, therefore to discontinue monitoring as requested by registrar. No contact from parents throughout shift."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then, as his Lordship has already pointed out, your name and the date.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just looking at that entry:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Pre-feed blood glucose all above 2 mol, therefore discontinue monitoring."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Does that remind you of how [Baby L] presented at the start or through the early part of your shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. If I've written that, it would mean that his blood glucoses would have been all above 2 millimoles.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Okay. Were, do you remember, blood glucose levels at that stage, or were they, an issue for [Baby L]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think they had been because it was -- the baby was on a glucose infusion, but I can't remember, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Okay. The significance of any of those readings being over 2 mol on those occasions that you've noted? Is there any significance in those numbers?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because that's what a normal expectation would be, so we would want it to be above that.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: So certainly as far as your shift was concerned, you were satisfied that they were normal readings?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: All right, thank you. Could we go, please, to tile 54 next, Mr Murphy? We'll just deal with the observations, if we may, that you recorded on that shift with [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down, please, to the bottom. If you could identify for us if your signature or your initials in your hand appear on the bottom of that page?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Are they the -- it looks like a T and they're pretty well in the middle on six of those boxes; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: We'll come to possibly later ones in a moment, but if we just concentrate on those, please. We've become more familiar with this sort of document. Is this something you recognise?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Does it represent the observations, if we scroll down, that you took over that period of baby [Baby L]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: My Lord, this document is in the paper bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I'm not going to dwell on it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is there anything there, Nurse Jones, that strikes you as unusual or that you feel you need to bring to our attention during that part of your shift?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Scroll it up again, please.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: All the entries appear to be within the necessary parameters?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: And then there's some handwritten entries further down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Saturations --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: -- all except one, I think, at 100. Then you've ticked affirmatively the various checks that you had to make and we can see the temperature of the cot as well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Going back to those blood glucose levels that you told us about, can we go next, please, to tile 55, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, that form that you are familiar with or do you recall from the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause). Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Take a moment. It specifies in the top right, Countess of Chester, is it something similar --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Okay. Then can I ask, towards the top left of the document where we can see "Twin 1 [Surname of Babies L & M]", which we know was [Baby L], are they your initials in those boxes on the top left?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: To confirm that you've done those checks?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. Then if we look at the times, which are about a third of the way down the page as we look at it now, from 20.00 we have hourly boxes; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Which, as [Baby L]'s designated nurse, you'd have been responsible for completing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Again, I'm not going to ask you about any of those higher entries, but if we could scroll down to those nearer the middle of the page. Along the line of
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "feeds", there are entries, 2.3, 2.2, and is that a 3.6?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: What do they represent, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They would have been the blood glucose levels that I took.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Certainly above the second and third is the word "pre"; does that tell us anything?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's pre-feed.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: So the level would be taken before [Baby L] fed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Can we see from that particular feed row that [Baby L] was receiving donor-expressed breast milk two-hourly; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: And certainly the three entries on the right, which appear to be yours, correct me if I'm wrong, are via an NGT?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Is that 7ml, then 8ml, then 7?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: And then a cumulative figure underneath?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. If we scroll down -- sorry, before we do, that top row, is that a rolling record of the fluids that [Baby L] was receiving intravenously --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: -- in addition to milk?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Somebody's noted 10% glucose --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: -- by way of explanation? All right, thank you. Now if we can scroll down. Is that your handwriting, "Mec and PU"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Confirming your note that meconium had been passed and urine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. If we can go, please, to the next -- that one finishes at midnight.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can go to tile 70, please, for the next fluid balance chart. Again, my Lord, these are in the jury's paper bundle.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm following it on paper. It's much easier because you can see the whole document.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry, I'm tied to the screen, I do apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, no. It's near to the back of it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So same form but we can see the date towards the top left, now 9 April. If we scroll down to the bottom, please. Are you able to identify your initials again?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: We can see that they're timed at 2 am, 4 am and 6 am, those columns?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. In a similar fashion, we can see the milk feeds continuing via NGT; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: We can see on each occasion 7ml; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: And the cumulative figures start again because we pass midnight?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Fluids are continuing in that top row; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: And again, as far as output is concerned, on two occasions you've entered "passed urine" and the first -- is that "bowel not opened"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: But at 6 am meconium?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: All right. I note, please tell me if I'm wrong, on those entries between 1 am and 6 am, you haven't continued to record the blood sugars. Does that follow on from what you told us earlier?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think in the notes it had said that because they were normal, we didn't need to continue doing that.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: All right. So we've got those three readings you talk about in your note and because of the readings that you got, that regular monitoring was able to stop.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Before we move on from blood sugars, please, could we just have a look behind tile 5, Mr Murphy, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'll ask you to look at a form which you may or may not recognise. In fact, we can see the first four entries are not your initials, but are the next two yours?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: They're not dated, but probably because they -- do they follow on from the 8th?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, they match the blood sugars in my notes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: And I think those three readings, even though the third is undated -- certainly the first two follow your entries on the feeding chart that we've just been looking at?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: I'm afraid the third isn't dated so I don't know whether that's the same one or not. Are any of those entries yours other than those two that we've looked at?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't tell because there isn't -- my signature isn't there.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Can we scroll down a little bit more, Mr Murphy, so we can see the whole thing? I don't think there are, but you tell us if I'm wrong. Just those two entries with your initials?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's all I can see, yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. Tile 74 next, please, Mr Murphy. We don't need to go behind these. I think you mentioned that it would have been the ward staff who administered medication so when we see at 3.41, benzylpenicillin being administered, is that consistent with what you told us earlier, whereby members of the ward staff would provide those drugs to the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: All right. I know, because we looked at the initials on the computer, that in fact a nurse with the initials BB was on duty that night. So it may be that she was the lady who admitted you to the computer to make your note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Very likely.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Did you at any point during the course of that shift have any cause to change any of the IV bags that [Baby L] was attached to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, not from my recollection.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Can we look, please, at the next night shift and go to tile 200. We can see that you came on again at the same time the following night. Again, were you [Baby L]'s designated nurse that night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Let's go to your notes, please, at tile 247. We'll check it is your note, please. No, that isn't your note, I'm afraid. Let's just have a look. It's over to the left, Mr Murphy. Thank you. Down a bit.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So into the morning of the 10th now. You've written a similar time to your note the night before, would that be fair to say?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: This time we've the initials [Initials of Nurse C]. I think there was a nurse by the name of [Nurse C] on that night.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So do you imagine it was the same situation where they opened the computer up for you and you made the notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we look at your note then, please:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Care taken over at 19.30 hours by Tracey Jones, agency nurse. All safety checks completed and satisfactory. Baby currently nursed in an incubator in air. Full monitoring in situ and alarm limits set. At the start of the shift baby [Surname of Babies L & M] was on IV 12.5% dextrose [obviously higher the night before when you'd last cared for him] via peripheral cannula."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And was now nil by mouth, so no continuing milk feeds:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Blood sugars ranged from 2 to 2.4 through the night. [Dr A] informed and commenced some enteral feed of donor milk 3ml each 2 hours."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then you have noted that that intravenous infusion changed to a concentration of 15% at 6ml per hour and a long line was sited for infusion:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Blood sugar currently..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that would have been around, what, 4.48, when you made the note; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: "... 2.3 mols with dextrose 15% infusing. [Dr A] informed and requested I continue with the current fluid regime. Antibiotics administered as prescribed."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And just explain to us what "pre-gent level" means, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Gentamicin is one of the antibiotics. We have to measure the levels pre the administration, before.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: The levels of what?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Of the gentamicin.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Right, okay, thank you. Would that have been the situation as per the night before, that another member of staff would administer the antibiotic?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, because it's only -- the pre-levels are only sent on a certain regime, so it's not every administration.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Right, okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Temperature maintained and all observations within normal limits for gestation. Again, passed urine and meconium. Both parents visited and had cuddles."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then again you've written your name and dated it at the end. Having read that, any particular recollection of the shift with [Baby L], that second night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Only a brief recollection. It's a long time ago.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Okay. Perhaps if we go then to your observations chart at 202, please. Scroll down, please, Mr Murphy, to the initials at the bottom.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see -- we looked at this form earlier -- your initials in the centre of the page at the bottom there from the night shift before. Then I'm afraid the number is rather obscured, but do they appear to be your initials in those three boxes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Is that your handwriting above?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Immediately above that numbering, is that a reference to -- is that blood pressure?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Any reason why that, can you recall, is noted there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I probably would have just done that routinely.
blocks.speaker: JONES

blocks.text: Okay. You've written across the lower rows

blocks.text: By getting a new bag -- you do it sterilely, ie gowns, glove, mask. You get a new bag of fluids and withdraw so much of, say, your 10%, and then you add the measured amount of 50% to get it to the right proportion, all of which is worked out by pharmacy.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Can we return to that in a minute because I'm going to ask you in a bit more detail about that process because I think there came a point in the shift where that became necessary; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. I don't want to run ahead too quickly. Can we look at tile 98, next, which is your note of the shift.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'd like to go through that with you before we break it down into individual entries. It runs across two pages.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can look at the start of the note, please, we can see your initials. This is made in retrospect, is that right, at the end of the day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Was it a busy day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So we can see there the note began at 20.58 and ended at 21.25. I'm going to go through it with you if I may:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Care taken over at 07.45. Equipment alarm, limits and fluids checked. At start of shift baby self-ventilating in air. Observations stable and satisfactory. Fluids increased to 75ml per kilogram."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is what we were talking about before with the pump, is that an adjustment on the pump?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: "2 times 12 and tolerated."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are they the milk feeds --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, they are the milk feeds.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: -- each 2 hours and obviously 12 in any 24-hour period?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You've noted that [Baby L] passed meconium and urine.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Then at 10 o'clock:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Blood taken for SBR and blood sugar."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: SBR, is that the bilirubin level?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Was [Baby L] being treated for jaundice?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So that's being monitored. You've also, is this right, taken a test for checking the blood sugar at 10?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Of the SBR, you entered -- is that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "58 and not far enough below the line, so phototherapy continued"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So the reading was such that the treatment carried on?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: It wasn't at a sufficient level to stop that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: You recorded the blood sugar at 1.9. What does that tell you, that sort of figure?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That the blood sugar was low and needed some intervention.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And hence, I think your next entry:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Intravenous dextrose increased to 2ml per kilogram"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Is that increased by 2ml per kilogram?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, it says "increased to".
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. Again, is that a setting on the pump?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Although that doesn't read right -- yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. But it represents an increase, does it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: You then repeated the blood sugar at 11?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And is this right, despite the additional dextrose, it's lower --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: -- at 1.6.? Is that, in your experience, what you would expect to find when you've given the baby more sugar?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: With prems you never know which way it'll go, but it was quite a shock. I didn't expect it to have fallen.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Right. Is this right, as a consequence that intravenous dextrose was further increased, according to your note, to 3ml per kilogram?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So that's the reading at 11. You've then put:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Blood sugar 1 hour later, 1.6."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So same level again --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: -- despite the further increase?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: What time, it might seem obvious, would that test have been?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... It'd probably have been -- the other one was at 11. It probably would have been 12, I would have thought.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. Your entry then is:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Blood taken for lab..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: "... but due to emergency not podded at once."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So who would have taken that sample?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would have taken it. But because I was in nursery 1, someone else would have been responsible -- it'd have been handed to someone else to pod.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Just dealing with the first part, how would you have taken it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A heel prick.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. How many samples would you have taken at that stage, do you know?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If it was just for the blood sugar, one.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: If you're testing for other things, do you have to take more than one?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It depends what you're testing for as to how many bottles you need.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Do you have any recollection of how many samples you took?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: All right. What time do you think you did -- you took that sample?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know unless it was on the notes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. In those circumstances and in your experience, how urgent is the taking of that blood sample?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, very urgent. I mean, he was having hourly blood sugars, so the likelihood is that would have been taken an hour after the last one.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So you've taken three readings. The third reading has prompted the requirement for a lab test?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Who would have ordered the lab test?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The doctors.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Do you happen to remember which doctor in this particular case?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. You'd have taken it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: You'd have treated it as -- would you have treated it as urgent?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Forgive me, I've no idea, but in these circumstances urgent could mean different things to different people.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are we talking before the end of the shift, are we talking in the next 30 seconds or somewhere in between?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Somewhere in between. The reason it was going to the lab was sometimes our machines on the unit, if they're not calibrated right and if you have several low readings, you send it to the lab to see what the lab's going to say, if it's going
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: to agree or if it's the machines on the unit that might not be...
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. So in situations such as this, what would your practice normally be? How soon would you hope to have done it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I hoped it would have gone, but after this I was called to another emergency, so I was unaware that it hadn't gone.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: That emergency came, what, after or before you'd taken the blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: All right. So just concentrating on the period between midday and that emergency, are you able to help us with how soon you expect you'd have taken it, the sample?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I can't, not this far back.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Do you remember anything about the emergency that you were called to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: We may come to it again shortly but what was the emergency you were called to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: His twin brother collapsed.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So you'd taken the sample. You said you handed it to someone else to pod; is that what you told us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Just tell us a little bit about podding before we move on.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's an air-driven system and it goes into a plastic pod and there's a chute and it goes straight to the lab.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Like supermarkets used to have for cash --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: -- in a capsule? Okay. So you'd have handed it to someone else to do that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: All right. When the emergency happened, had you handed it over at that point? Was that why there was a delay?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I've no idea. I can't remember that far back.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. So the emergency that caused the delay was the events with [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I suppose so. I mean, I wasn't aware that it hadn't been podded until I dealt with his brother and realised that the results had only just come on to the system.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. Do you know where the blood would have been in that period of time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Again, we'll come to [Baby M] in a moment, but just concentrating on this blood sample, you said you didn't know that it hadn't been podded until after [Baby M]'s incident.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. A colleague took over the care of [Baby L] because obviously I couldn't deal with two sick babies at the same time, so a colleague took over his care while I dealt with the other twin and then later in the shift I took him back.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: I just want to focus on the blood first, please, and then we'll come to that. So taken before [Baby M]'s collapse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: But not podded until after the collapse when you became aware it hadn't been done?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't guarantee that because, as I say, I was tied up elsewhere. All I know is the blood was taken. I can't enlarge any further on it.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. Do you happen to know who podded it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Can I ask you to look, please -- were you made aware of the results of that blood test at any point on your shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not until later on in the evening.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: When you took the sample, do you remember what sort of vessel it would have gone into?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A blood bottle.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And having taken the sample, what do you do with the blood bottle?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Put it in a paper envelope with a sticky label with the child's details on.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So you take the sample -- is it in a vial? I'm imagining a vial.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, a small vial, a plastic bottle.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Is the vial itself labelled?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: With what?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The patient's details.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Is that something that's done at the time the test is taken?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So blood is taken into the vial, label on the vial?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Then goes into a bag?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Again, does this happen when the sample's just been taken or does this take place further down the line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Usually when it's taken and the -- it would have been ordered -- the thing for the lab would have been ordered and you get a sticky label that you put on there with all the details and the lab number and then it goes off to the lab.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So the blood test is ordered by the doctor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: This document that you tell us with the sticky label on is generated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Generated, yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Do you get that before you take the blood test?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It depends.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: You take the blood test, you put a label on the vial itself. You put it in a bag and is it a different type of label that goes on the bag?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's just a large sticky label that comes off the printer.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: What's on the label?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The child's name, hospital number, what's required and the details of the doctor, whoever's ordered it.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Who checks that the relevant label is going on the right vial?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The person who's taken the blood.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Is that what you'd have done on this occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Sorry, I thought I'd covered this, but when that document with the sticker on is generated, who generates it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The order is done for -- whatever test you want is done on the computer and then it's automatically generated as the order is done and it comes off the printer.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And where is the printer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At the side of the computer.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And where's the computer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It depends which one you use. It could be in one of the nurseries or at the nursing station.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: But it's within the NNU?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: All right. So you've helped us with the process and how it's labelled and how it's podded. Tell us then, please, about what happened with [Baby M]. Where were you, can you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In nursery 1 with him.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall what you were doing at the time that [Baby M] collapsed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I was making a 12.5% dextrose for his brother.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: I think we touched on this earlier on. You told us that the bags have a preset concentration.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: If it's to be increased, there has to be a procedure undertaken by one of the nurses on the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And the calculations come from the pharmacy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: A new bag has to be used because, did you say, you don't know how much is --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You don't know how much is in the old bag so you don't know if you're going to get the right concentration, so you have to take a new bag.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So you have to get a new bag and then you have to carry out the process of, what, adding something?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have to become sterile. So you gown, glove, mask.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: You remove so much of the 10% dextrose that's in the bag, a measured amount which the pharmacy's told you, discard that, and then from a bottle of 50% dextrose, you withdraw so much and add to the 10% bag, mix it, and then you end up with 12.5%.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there. We've seen a video of this and I'm going to play it again. I'd like you to watch it and confirm if it's the process you're describing to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Video played to the court)
So is that the process that you were describing to us?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And that's the process you were undertaking in nursery 1 when [Baby M] collapsed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: All right. I think you mentioned that you have to -you're sterile; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: What does that involve, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Rigorous handwashing, mask, gloves and an apron, and I would have been working on a trolley with a sterile towel.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: How long does it take you to become sterile? Does it take...?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh, I don't know, 10 minutes, I suppose, if you wash your hands thoroughly.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: So 10 minutes before the procedure starts?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Was that a fair estimate when we watched the video of how long the process takes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, but you didn't see her gown-up.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Of course. Apart from the gowning-up?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: How long do you think you were occupied between gowning-up, finding the calculations, and starting to transfer the stronger solution into the --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I wouldn't know. It's impossible to remember things like that.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: All right. Could you just confirm, who was doing that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was doing the procedure.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: What happened then when [Baby M] collapsed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was with me because she was my checker, so she wouldn't have been gowned up. His alarms went, so she went to see what the problem was, because obviously I was sterile. And she said, "We need help over here".
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: At that point Belinda Simcock was in the nursery, so she said to me, "Mary, you go and sort the other twin out and I'll make sure that this is finished and goes up", and she took over the care
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: of [Baby L] at that point because obviously I couldn't be concerned with two potentially unstable babies.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Lucy was in the room when it happened?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Had she been in the room while you'd been gowning-up?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, yes, she'd have been with me the whole time because it's a two-check procedure.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: But only one person can --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Only one person does it, yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: -- (overspeaking) the glucose into the bag. We saw on the video that the glucose was delivered using a syringe into a port.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Do all the dextrose bags have that port for delivery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And what happens, we can see the syringe go in, what happens when the syringe is drawn out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It self-seals.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. Presumably, with a new bag having been prepared, and you told us that Belinda came in and took over, is that when -- would that new bag then have been hung while you were or shortly after you were dealing with [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: What's the procedure with the giving set that you mentioned to us earlier? Would that be changed as well or not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a form with the results of the blood gas on in a minute. But before I do, can I just go back to the process whereby the sample is taken and the labels are generated just so I understand it, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: You told us that the doctor orders the blood test.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Who goes on to the computer to generate the necessary actions thereafter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, whoever's ordering the blood. Some of the nurses can order it, depending what the test is. The order goes in and the form is automatically generated.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. But what I'm asking is who goes on the computer to set that train in motion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Whoever's ordering.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Right, okay. Is it always the nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. For some tests, it's the doctors that do it. It just depends. It could be a doctor or some nurses can do it.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: It's only after that's been entered into the computer by the doctor or the nurse that the documentation is printed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Including the labels?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: For the label on the bottle you can use a patient label.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Okay. Was it your practice to put that label on before or after the blood was entered into the vial?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Would you have it available when you'd taken the blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Mr Astbury, we're coming up to break time.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't know how long you're likely to be. Unless you're going to be a few minutes, I think we'll have the break now.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If that's a convenient time. All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We just have a ten-minute break in the middle of the morning, so you may have a ten-minute break. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Ten minutes then, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)

You helpfully, Nurse Griffith, took us through that process that was going on in nursery 1 at the time that [Baby M] collapsed. And before I move on, could we just have a look, please, at the events of the afternoon that led you to that point where the dextrose bag was having to be increased further. If we can go to tile 97, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Earlier, we identified your initials at the bottom of that particular document and we can see that by reading up, your entries span from 08.00 until 15.00; is that right? They are certainly your initials and then I think a couple afterwards later in the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Somebody's helped at 16.00, have they?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: Then you continue for another three entries there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: I'm looking in the leftmost column where you've handwritten "BMs". Can you see that? It's about three-quarters of the way down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITH

blocks.text: And you've handwritten "BMs". Then there are a series of readings across the afternoon or the day shift. I'd just like to go through those with you. You have told us about some of the entries, the 1.9 at 10. You told us about a 1.6 at 11, which isn't on there, but you put in your nursing notes. There's another 1.6 at 12 o'clock; is that right?

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: that reference range. But that again is a normal result because growth hormone is sometimes produced in response to low blood sugar. They get separated from each other when the insulin is secreted by the pancreas into the bloodstream. So you can measure both the insulin level and the C-peptide level.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The C-peptide level is usually higher than, considerably higher than, the insulin level simply because insulin gets removed rapidly from the body in the liver. The C-peptide lasts longer in the bloodstream, so the C-peptide level -- sorry, although from the pancreas, as they're secreted, there should be an equal amount inside the pancreas of C-peptide and insulin, inside the circulating blood C-peptide is higher than insulin.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS
